Name: Distributed Monolith
Symptom: All services must deploy together; one failure cascades everywhere
Root Cause: Tight coupling between services via shared DB, synchronous calls, or shared libraries
Why It's Tempting: Microservices architecture promised independence but teams kept the coupling
Fix: Define clear service boundaries with async communication; use API contracts; eliminate shared mutable state
Related Patterns: Bounded Context, Event-Driven Architecture, API Gateway
Keywords: distributed monolith coupling deploy together cascade shared db

Name: Shared Database Integration
Symptom: Schema changes break multiple services; teams block each other on migrations
Root Cause: Multiple services read/write the same database tables directly
Why It's Tempting: Fastest way to share data — no API to build
Fix: Give each service its own schema/database; use events or APIs for cross-service data; apply CDC for migration
Related Patterns: Database per Service, Event-Driven, CDC, Strangler Fig
Keywords: shared database integration coupling schema migration

Name: God Service
Symptom: One service handles 80%+ of traffic and business logic; single point of failure
Root Cause: Incremental feature additions without decomposition; lack of domain boundaries
Why It's Tempting: Easier to add to existing service than create new infrastructure
Fix: Identify bounded contexts; extract services along domain boundaries; use strangler fig pattern
Related Patterns: Bounded Context, Strangler Fig, Single Responsibility
Keywords: god service monolith single point failure bloated

Name: Sync-over-Async
Symptom: Thread pool exhaustion; latency spikes under load; cascading timeouts
Root Cause: Blocking synchronous calls wrapped in async frameworks or chained across services
Why It's Tempting: Synchronous is simpler to reason about and debug
Fix: Use truly async I/O; apply backpressure; set timeouts and circuit breakers on all remote calls
Keywords: sync over async blocking thread pool exhaustion latency timeout

Name: Dual Writes
Symptom: Data inconsistency between database and message broker; lost events
Root Cause: Writing to two systems (e.g. DB + Kafka) without atomicity — one write can fail while the other succeeds
Why It's Tempting: Simpler than setting up outbox/CDC; appears to work in happy path
Fix: Use Transactional Outbox pattern; use CDC (Debezium); use event sourcing where writes and events are one operation
Related Patterns: Transactional Outbox, CDC, Event Sourcing, Saga
Keywords: dual writes inconsistency database broker atomicity outbox

Name: Chatty Microservices
Symptom: High latency due to many inter-service calls per request; network overhead dominates
Root Cause: Over-decomposed services requiring multiple round-trips to fulfill one user request
Why It's Tempting: Fine-grained services seemed aligned with single responsibility principle
Fix: Merge overly granular services; use API composition/BFF pattern; batch calls; cache aggressively
Related Patterns: API Gateway, BFF, CQRS, Materialized View
Keywords: chatty microservices network latency round trip overhead

Name: Unbounded Retry
Symptom: Thundering herd on recovery; downstream overwhelmed; cascading failures
Root Cause: Retry loops without backoff, jitter, or max-attempt limits
Why It's Tempting: Retries seem like the simplest way to handle transient errors
Fix: Add exponential backoff with jitter; set max retries; use circuit breakers; implement dead-letter queues
Related Patterns: Circuit Breaker, Exponential Backoff, Dead Letter Queue
Keywords: unbounded retry thundering herd backoff jitter max attempts

Name: Missing Idempotency Key
Symptom: Duplicate orders/payments/messages on retry; data corruption
Root Cause: No deduplication mechanism; retries re-execute side effects
Why It's Tempting: Idempotency adds complexity; happy path works without it
Fix: Add idempotency keys to all mutating APIs; use database unique constraints; deduplicate at consumer level
Related Patterns: Idempotent Consumer, Transactional Outbox, At-Least-Once Delivery
Keywords: idempotency key duplicate retry deduplication side effect

Name: Premature Microservices
Symptom: Slow development velocity; excessive operational overhead for team size; unclear boundaries
Root Cause: Adopting microservices before understanding domain boundaries or having the team/infra to support them
Why It's Tempting: Microservices are trendy; architecture astronauting; resume-driven development
Fix: Start with a well-structured modular monolith; extract services only when you have clear bounded contexts and operational maturity
Related Patterns: Modular Monolith, Bounded Context, Strangler Fig
Keywords: premature microservices monolith team size operational overhead

Name: Log-and-Throw
Symptom: Duplicate log entries for the same error; noise drowns signal; confusing stack traces
Root Cause: Catching an exception, logging it, then re-throwing — each layer logs the same error
Why It's Tempting: Feels safe — 'at least we logged it'
Fix: Log at the boundary (entry point) only; use structured error context; propagate errors with context, don't log-and-rethrow
Related Patterns: Error Boundary, Structured Logging, Exception Handling
Keywords: log and throw duplicate logging noise rethrow exception

Name: Generic Error Swallowing
Symptom: Silent failures; data loss; impossible to debug production issues
Root Cause: Catching broad exceptions (catch Exception / catch all) and ignoring or logging without action
Fix: Catch specific exceptions; fail fast on unexpected errors; use error boundaries at well-defined layers; alert on swallowed errors
Related Patterns: Fail Fast, Error Boundary, Circuit Breaker
Keywords: error swallowing catch all silent failure exception broad

Name: N+1 Query
Symptom: Endpoint latency grows linearly with collection size; excessive DB queries in traces
Root Cause: ORM lazy-loads relations per row instead of batching
Why It's Tempting: ORMs default to lazy loading; works fine with small datasets
Fix: Eager-load relations (JOIN / prefetch_related); use DataLoader for GraphQL; batch IDs in WHERE IN clause
Keywords: n+1 query orm lazy load dataloader prefetch eager

Name: Secrets in Environment Variables
Symptom: Secrets visible in process listing, container inspect, crash dumps, CI logs
Root Cause: Storing sensitive values as plain-text env vars without encryption or rotation
Why It's Tempting: 12-factor app recommends config via env vars; simple to implement
Fix: Use a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager); mount secrets as files; rotate regularly
Related Patterns: Vault, KMS, Secret Rotation, Zero Trust
Keywords: secrets environment variables env var plaintext vault kms

Name: Time-Based Cache Invalidation Only
Symptom: Stale data served to users; inconsistency window equals TTL; cache stampede on expiry
Root Cause: Relying solely on TTL for cache freshness without event-driven invalidation
Why It's Tempting: TTL is the simplest caching strategy; works for read-heavy low-consistency needs
Fix: Combine TTL with event-driven invalidation (CDC, pub/sub); use cache-aside with write-through; implement stale-while-revalidate
Keywords: cache invalidation ttl stale stampede event driven

Name: Polling Instead of Events
Symptom: Wasted resources; delayed reactions; high DB load from repeated queries
Root Cause: Using periodic polling instead of event-driven notifications for state changes
Why It's Tempting: Polling is simpler to implement; no messaging infrastructure needed
Fix: Use webhooks, CDC, or message brokers for push-based notifications; reserve polling for legacy integrations only
Related Patterns: Event-Driven Architecture, CDC, Webhooks, Message Broker
Keywords: polling instead events webhook cdc push notification wasted resources
